compatibility.title: Which BMW Models Use the M60B30?
compatibility.intro: The M60B30 was BMW's first V8 engine to appear in the 5 Series and the first V8 in the 7 Series since the 1970s. It produced 215 bhp - significantly more than the straight‑six it replaced - and was offered in both the E34 5 Series and E38 7 Series throughout the mid‑1990s.

costGuide.title: BMW M60B30 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an M60B30 typically takes 12-14 hours at £65-£75/hr (independent BMW specialist). Main dealer rates are no longer applicable for this engine as BMW no longer supports it through main dealer channels.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the Nikasil cylinder linings - engines that survived the UK high‑sulphur fuel era are more desirable, but many were affected. The condition of the cooling system (water pump, radiator, thermostat) also significantly affects value, as well-maintained examples command a premium. failures.title: BMW M60B30 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Nikasil Cylinder Lining Wear - bore scoring and compression loss
items.whatHappens: The M60B30 - like all M60 engines - features Nikasil (nickel‑silicon‑carbide) cylinder coatings. High‑sulphur UK petrol of the 1990s was a known issue for these linings, causing them to wear prematurely. This leads to bore scoring, loss of compression, increased oil consumption, and eventually engine failure. BMW identified the issue and, from 1996 onward, switched to Alusil linings for the M62 family. The M60B30 suffered proportionately less than the larger M60B40, but affected examples were still common in the UK.
items.repairVsReplace: If bore scoring is caught early, re‑honing and re‑coating the Nikasil liners is possible (£1,500-£3,000) but requires specialist equipment. If the engine has lost compression on multiple cylinders, a replacement unit is almost always more cost‑effective. Read our full cylinder wear guide

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - water pump, radiator, and thermostat housing
items.whatHappens: The M60's cooling system is a known weak point, with the water pump, radiator, and thermostat housing all prone to leaks and failure. The water pump impeller can fail, the plastic radiator end tanks crack, and the thermostat housing can warp - leading to coolant loss, overheating, and potential head gasket failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump and thermostat replacement typically resolves the issue (£400-£800 at an independent specialist). If overheating is ignored, head gasket failure can occur (£1,000-£2,500 to repair), or in severe cases, cylinder head damage requiring full engine replacement. Read our full cooling system failure guide

items.title: Oil Leaks - valve cover gaskets, timing cover, and sump gasket
items.whatHappens: The M60's gaskets harden and shrink over time, leading to oil leaks from the valve cover gaskets, timing cover, and sump pan. Oil leaks can drip onto the exhaust manifolds, producing a burning oil smell, and can lead to low oil levels if left unchecked.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve cover gasket replacement is straightforward (£300-£600); timing cover and sump gasket replacement is more labour‑intensive (£600-£1,200). If oil leaks are ignored, low oil levels can lead to bearing wear and eventual engine failure.

variants.title: M60 Sub‑Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The M60 family consists of several variants, differentiated primarily by displacement, configuration, and output. The M60B30 sits alongside the larger M60B40 in the M60 V8 line‑up. - Fitted to: BMW E34 530i (1992-1996), BMW E38 730i (1994-1997) - Key technical difference: 3.0L capacity (76mm bore × 82.7mm stroke), double VANOS on intake camshaft, Nikasil cylinder linings - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the Nikasil cylinder lining wear issue common to all M60 engines; the 3.0L version is less prone to bore scoring than the 4.0L M60B40 due to lower specific output - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the M60B40 (4.0L); ECU, engine mounts, and exhaust manifold differ - Fitted to: BMW E32 740i, E34 540i, E38 740i (1992-1997) - Key technical difference: 4.0L capacity (89mm bore × 80mm stroke), same Nikasil linings, higher output - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: The 4.0L M60B40 is more prone to Nikasil bore scoring than the 3.0L due to higher cylinder pressures - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with M60B30; ECU, engine mounts, and exhaust manifold differ; engine bay space is similar but wiring and cooling system plumbing are different The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the cylinder block, visible from the driver's side of the engine bay, and appears on the V5C registration document. Alternatively, enter your registration above - we'll confirm your exact fitment.

- the 3.5L V8 that replaced the M60B30 in the E39 5 Series and E38 7 Series from 1996; it features Alusil linings (addressing the Nikasil issue), increased displacement, and improved torque delivery. This is the natural upgrade for M60B30 owners, though ECU and cooling system differences mean it's not a simple swap.

If you're looking for more power, this is the engine to consider - but it requires a different ECU and exhaust system.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement M60B30 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used M60B30 can make sense for owners of lower‑value E34 530i or E38 730i examples where a reconditioned unit would exceed the vehicle's value. However, used units carry significant risk: you don't know the Nikasil lining condition, cooling system history, or oil leak severity. Only consider a used unit with documented service history and a compression test. Expect to pay £500-£1,200 for a used M60B30.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: For most M60B30 replacements, a professionally reconditioned unit is the right call. A proper recon addresses the engine's known weak points: the cooling system (water pump, radiator, thermostat) is overhauled, all gaskets and seals are renewed, and - crucially - the Nikasil linings are inspected and re‑coated if necessary. With a 12‑24 month warranty, this is the lowest‑risk option for a £1,800-£3,000+ investment.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for this engine only when the original block is in good condition and the vehicle has significant sentimental or collector value - e.g. a low‑mileage E38 730i or a well‑specified E34 530i. A rebuild allows for upgraded internals and conversion to Alusil liners, but for most owners, a reconditioned exchange unit offers better value and less downtime. Expect £2,500-£4,500+ for a full rebuild.

items.question: What are the common problems with the M60B30?
items.answer: The most significant issue is Nikasil cylinder lining wear, caused by high‑sulphur UK petrol in the 1990s, leading to bore scoring, compression loss and oil consumption. Cooling system failures (water pump, radiator, thermostat) and oil leaks (valve cover gaskets, timing cover) are also very common on higher‑mileage examples. A compression test is essential before buying any M60B30. Consider proactively replacing the cooling system if you're investing in a replacement engine.

It was BMW's first V8 in the 5 Series and the first V8 in the 7 Series since the 1970s, producing 215 bhp and offering a significant power increase over the straight‑six it replaced. items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt M60B30?
items.answer: For most owners, a reconditioned unit offers the best balance - it includes new cooling system components, all gaskets replaced, and crucially, the Nikasil linings inspected and re‑coated if necessary. Used units are cheaper but carry significant Nikasil risk; full rebuilds are justified only for high‑value or collector cars. Reconditioned from £1,800; used from £500; rebuilt from £2,500. Always request documented proof of cylinder condition and which parts have been replaced.

items.question: How do I tell the M60B30 apart from the M60B40?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the driver's side of the cylinder block, and appears on the V5C and in the VIN (digits 4‑7). The M60B30 is a 3.0L V8 producing 215 bhp; the M60B40 is a 4.0L V8 producing 282 bhp. They share the same architecture but have different bore/stroke, ECU calibration, and exhaust manifolds. The M60B40 is more prone to Nikasil bore scoring due to higher cylinder pressures. Fitting the wrong displacement variant requires a different ECU and engine loom.
bullets: The M60B40 is more prone to Nikasil bore scoring due to higher cylinder pressures.
Fitting the wrong displacement variant requires a different ECU and engine loom.

items.question: How reliable is the M60B30 compared to later BMW V8s?
items.answer: The M60B30 is generally less reliable than the later M62 family (Alusil linings) and significantly less reliable than the N63/S63 generations that followed. The Nikasil issue is the primary concern; if the engine has survived without bore scoring, it can be relatively robust with proper maintenance. However, cooling system and oil leak issues are still common. Regular servicing and cooling system inspection are critical. Many specialists recommend proactively replacing the water pump and thermostat on high‑mileage M60s.
